title: The Lost Medal of Oakwood School

nodes.body: You are helping Mrs Okonkwo clear the lost-property room on the last day of school. She is the school secretary. Three long tables fill the hall. They are covered with lost jumpers, lunchboxes and odd trainers. The hot lights shine down. Anything left by four o'clock will go to a charity shop. Inside a crate of mixed sports kit, your fingers close on something cold. It is a brass swimming medal. The edges are dull green. A name has been filed off the front. A tiny date is scratched inside the ribbon clasp.

choices.label: Twist the medal into the light and read the scratched date properly.

nodes.body: The clasp holds a single year, 1974, scratched deep. Folded into a tiny square and stuffed behind the ribbon is a piece of yellowed paper: a list of six initials and an event name, THE COUNTY FINALS, with four of the initials crossed out. Mrs Okonkwo checks the faded tag still tied to the ribbon loop. It says 'Found: Old Pool, 2002'. She tells you the old school pool was demolished years ago, filled in for the new drama block.

choices.label: Ask Mrs Okonkwo about the day the pool was emptied.
Start with the nearest place the medal might have come from.
Take the scrap of paper to the local library.

nodes.body: Mrs Okonkwo has cleared this school every July for eleven years. She remembers almost every strange thing she has ever found in a locker. She pulls a dog-eared blue folder from her filing cabinet. The pool was taken down in 2005. But all the old school trophies and sports records were boxed up. They were put into the boiler-room store. One of those boxes has never been fully sorted.

choices.label: Ask to look at the unopened trophy box.
Study the old pool photographs hanging in the corridor.
Ask if you can still get into the old boiler room.

nodes.body: You hold the medal up to the grey window light. The scratch lines on the clasp connect to a faint map you did not see before. It is a map of six small dots around the old school grounds. A wavy line links them. The nearest dot sits where the old pool door used to be. This is now a bike shed. It has a bumpy plastic roof. A broken clock hangs over the door where the pool hours used to be.

choices.label: Go and look at the bike shed properly.
Follow the wavy line around the school field.
Check the old viewing gallery steps.

nodes.body: The town library keeps the old school files on one metal shelf. Ask for the grey box marked 'Oakwood: Sports 1960-1990'. Nobody has opened it for about twenty years. Mr Chen is the librarian. He has his lunch at exactly half past twelve. He would love it if someone asked him a question that needs more than a quick web search.

choices.label: Work through the grey sports archive box.
Get the microfilm reader going.
Ask Mr Chen what he already knows.

nodes.body: The boiler-room store smells of damp plaster and old plimsolls. Under a stack of gym mats sits the trophy box: a dusty cardboard crate. Inside are a faded swimming cap with the school logo, two team photographs with names inked on the back, and a brown envelope of receipts for pool chemicals, a stopwatch repair and one re-plastered diving board.

choices.label: Work out who the initials on the paper belong to.
Study the receipts for dates and details.
Take the swimming cap to someone who might recognise it.

nodes.body: Two black-and-white photographs show a swim team standing on tiled steps somewhere in the school. Twenty-two children in caps, holding medals. On the back of one, in soft pencil, are twelve initials and the words 'COUNTY FINALS DAY'. The tiles in the picture are a distinctive cracked blue mosaic. They are not the tiles of the current school hall, and they are not anywhere obvious now.

choices.label: Work out who the initials belong to.
Study the receipts for dates and details.
Take the swimming cap to someone who might recognise it.

nodes.body: The old boiler room is strictly out of bounds. You cannot go in without a member of staff. The door is heavy. The key hangs on a hook in the secretary's office. Mrs Okonkwo will let you in with a nod if you ask her directly. But she will give you a very stern look if she catches you trying the handle on your own.

choices.label: Work out who the initials belong to.
Study the receipts for dates and details.
Take the swimming cap to someone who might recognise it.

nodes.body: The old pool door is a bike shed now. The air smells of damp trainers and tyre rubber. A strip of blue mosaic tiles is all that is left of the old doorway. The tiles are set into the concrete floor. There is also a patch of newer brick on the wall. Something small and square was once fixed there. Then it was taken down.

choices.label: Figure out what was fixed to that patch of wall.
Look under the layers of paint on the door frame.
Ask at the caretaker's office.

nodes.body: The wavy line scratched inside the clasp traces a route. It goes from the old pool to the far end of the playing field. Six dots sit along it. The distances do not match any modern school map. That is, unless you draw back in the old spectator path. It was covered with tarmac when the new science block went up.

choices.label: Figure out what was fixed to that patch of wall.
Look under the layers of paint on the door frame.
Ask at the caretaker's office.

nodes.body: The old viewing gallery steps are still there, painted grey over grey over grey. A small brass plaque on the wall beside them says 'OAKWOOD SCHOOL POOL 1965'. Beside it, a neat rectangle of empty screw holes shows where a second, smaller plaque very obviously used to be.

choices.label: Figure out what was fixed to that patch of wall.
Look under the layers of paint on the door frame.
Ask at the caretaker's office.

nodes.body: The grey box file holds a run of old school news sheets. The staples are rusted. There is a short bit in the faded July 1974 issue about the County Finals. It lists all six event spots. But the order does not match the list inside the medal clasp.

choices.label: Look at the small brass plaque in the library drawer.
Find the old school board minutes.
Find out exactly when the charity van is coming.

nodes.body: The microfilm reader eats twenty-pence pieces. It holds the 'Oakwood Observer' back to 1965. Every summer, the paper has a photo of the swim team. They stand in the sun with their medals. They squint into the camera like they are already remembering it.

choices.label: Look at the small brass plaque in the library drawer.
Find the old school board minutes.
Find out exactly when the charity van is coming.

nodes.body: Mr Chen has worked at this desk for nine years. He keeps a drawer of things people have handed in and never picked up. A small brass plaque is wrapped in a clean dust-cloth inside it. The plaque is the size of a playing card. It has four screw holes, a single initial, and no explanation at all.

choices.label: Look at the small brass plaque in the library drawer.
Find the old school board minutes.
Find out exactly when the charity van is coming.

nodes.body: There are twelve sets of initials on the back of a photo. Four of them still belong to people who work in this town. One is painted in gold above the dry-cleaner's on the high street. A set of initials on an old team photo is not a real person until you go and find them.

choices.label: Find out who the mystery swimmer was.
Go and find Miss Holloway.
Search the changing room block before four o'clock.

nodes.body: A receipt is a dull thing that cannot lie. There are chlorine tablets from 1989. A stopwatch was fixed in 1994. A locksmith was called out to the old starting-block store in November 1998. That was six weeks before the pool was drained for the last time.

choices.label: Put the six event locations into the right order.
Leave the box and come back tomorrow.
Find out who the mystery swimmer was.

nodes.body: The cap has the faded school logo and a tiny sewn-on badge of a diving figure. There are perhaps three people left in this town who would know it across a room. One of them lives in the old coach's cottage by the park, and one of them is Miss Holloway.

choices.label: Go and find Miss Holloway.
Search the changing room block before four o'clock.
Put the six event locations into the right order.

nodes.body: The patch of newer brick on the bike shed wall is the size of a playing card and has four filled screw holes in it. The brass plaque in the library is exactly that size. Somewhere in this school, there is a cupboard with five of these in it, or there was a skip in 2005 that took them all.

choices.label: Measure the scratch map against a real school map.
Go up to the old viewing gallery steps.
Try the old coach's cottage garden.

nodes.body: A plaque painted over five times is still a plaque. Its slight bump shows up under a raking torch beam. On the old pool route, there are two doorways where the paint sits on a square shape instead of lying flat. One of them is behind a 'Lost Property' sign screwed to the wall.

choices.label: Go and look at the old starting-block store.
Walk the whole route and leave it at that.
Measure the scratch map against a real school map.

nodes.body: The caretaker's office has a noticeboard screwed to the wall. It is at the same height a small plaque would sit. Mr Harris, the caretaker, has never looked behind it. The office is locked from eight until four. It is completely empty for his tea break at quarter past ten.

choices.label: Go up to the old viewing gallery steps.
Try the old coach's cottage garden.
Go and look at the old starting-block store.

nodes.body: The plaque says 'COUNTY FINALS: THIRD EVENT'. Under it is a single letter, 'P'. On the back, someone has scratched a name and a date in 2005. It came in with a bag of old school books. It has been in this drawer for nearly a year, waiting for this very question.

choices.label: Work out what the six initials on the paper are for.
Go and see Mr Harris at the caretaker's yard.
Search the Observer for the last Finals day.

nodes.body: The school board minutes live in a green ring-binder. They are as dull as anything ever typed. On page three of the September 2005 set is a single line. It is about clearing the store under the old starting block before the work to knock it down.

choices.label: Ring the number at the bottom of the minutes.
Build the file first and act on it later.
Work out what the six initials on the paper are for.

nodes.body: The charity van is booked for four o'clock today. The driver is on a tight schedule. A store that has been cleared is cleared. Whatever is still in the old starting-block cupboard goes into a van. Then it goes into a sorting depot. Nobody in the school will ever know what it was.

choices.label: Go and see Mr Harris at the caretaker's yard.
Search the Observer for the last Finals day.
Ring the number at the bottom of the minutes.

nodes.body: The mystery swimmer was a pupil called Patrick Keele. He swam the last part of the relay for five years. He kept every paper he was ever given. He left school with one shelf of trophies and no photo in the yearbook. His old classmates knew he was fast and not much else. That tells you its own kind of fact about a person.

choices.label: Go and look hard at the padlock on the store.
Work out what the six scratched initials must be.
Take everything you know to Miss Holloway.

nodes.body: Miss Holloway was the last team coach. She lives in the old school house on Sycamore Road. Everyone who speaks of her says the same two things in the same order. Her memory for names is going. And you should ask her anyway.

choices.label: Get Mr Harris to hold the charity van.
Get behind the noticeboard in the caretaker's office.
Ask at the old coach's cottage.

nodes.body: There is one hour left before the van arrives. The few places in the changing rooms still worth checking are these. The top of the old noticeboard. The back of the fuse cupboard. And the gap behind the bottom locker door. That is where everyone in every school has always put the thing they did not want thrown out.

choices.label: Ask about the locked cage in the caretaker's yard.
Get into the old viewing gallery.
Ask at the local museum about the medals.

nodes.body: The scrap of paper lists the six events in one order. The scratch marks on the medal clasp are different. Only one of those two orders is the order the swimmers really moved between events. The other is the order someone wrote them down later. They sat at a desk after it was all over.

choices.label: Write to the local paper.
Get Rafi and his bike into it.
Work backwards from four o'clock.

nodes.body: Laid over a proper printed map of the school with a ruler, five of the six dots land within thirty paces of a real place. The sixth dot lands in the middle of the new science block. Either the scratches are wrong, or the science block is standing on something.

choices.label: Go and look hard at the padlock on the store.
Work out what the six scratched initials must be.
Take everything you know to Miss Holloway.

nodes.body: The old viewing gallery steps are wide and worn. They are exactly the steps in the 1974 photo. The wall beside them has four filled screw holes at plaque height. They are plugged with a filler that dried a different shade of grey from the stone around it.

choices.label: Get Mr Harris to hold the charity van.
Get behind the noticeboard in the caretaker's office.
Ask at the old coach's cottage.

nodes.body: The old coach's cottage has a garden you can see through a gap in the hedge off the main drive. On its far wall, half-hidden behind a climbing rose that nobody has pruned since it was a good idea, is a small brass rectangle everyone stopped seeing years ago.

choices.label: Ask about the locked cage in the caretaker's yard.
Get into the old viewing gallery.
Ask at the local museum about the medals.

nodes.body: The starting-block store sits at the deep end of the filled-in pool, now a sunken garden. Its paint is flaking off. A heavy steel door is set into a brick arch under it. A six-letter padlock, green with age, hangs on the door. Someone tried to break it with a screwdriver and gave up.

choices.label: Write to the local paper.
Get Rafi and his bike into it.
Work backwards from four o'clock.

nodes.body: Six events, six plaques, one initial on each, and a six-letter padlock on a steel door. Four of the initials on the paper are crossed out in the same ink as the rest. That means someone tried them and got them wrong, rather than used them and moved on.

choices.label: Go and look hard at the padlock on the store.
Work out what the six scratched initials must be.
Take everything you know to Miss Holloway.

nodes.body: Mr Harris runs the whole site out of a cluttered yard behind the bike sheds. He has a clipboard, a master key, and a charity van booked for four o'clock. He has been told twice this year, by people senior to him, that everything in that old store is junk.

choices.label: Get Mr Harris to hold the charity van.
Get behind the noticeboard in the caretaker's office.
Ask at the old coach's cottage.

nodes.body: The last County Finals here were in the summer of 1998 under a grey drizzle. The 'Observer' gave it four column inches. It ran a photo of twelve swimmers where there had once been twenty-two.

choices.label: Ask about the locked cage in the caretaker's yard.
Get into the old viewing gallery.
Ask at the local museum about the medals.

nodes.body: The number on the minutes rings a desk at the council. That desk has moved departments twice. The person who answers is helpful but has no power. They can say with perfect clarity which other person is not.

choices.label: Write to the local paper.
Get Rafi and his bike into it.
Work backwards from four o'clock.

nodes.body: The trophy box goes to a charity sale at half past three. It goes with twelve other crates. By the time anyone knows what was inside, the cap, photos, and receipts are gone. They are in three different sorting rooms. The medal stays with you. The scrap of paper stays too. Everything else that could have proved anything is gone.

The six dots turn out to be six real spots, and the walk between them takes twenty minutes in the drizzle and answers nothing. Four blank walls, a bike shed, and a padlock. It is a very good map of a school that has been rebuilt, and the medal goes into your pocket.

ending.title: Six Dots and a Drizzly Lunchtime

nodes.body: By ten to four there is a folder holding the six events, the dates, the minutes, and a photocopy of the brass plaque. It is genuinely good work. The van comes at four all the same. The folder goes onto the local history shelf, where someone will find it in twenty years and wonder.

The door under the old starting block is steel set in brick, and the padlock is a six-letter combination gone green. It turns stiffly on the first two dials and more stiffly on the last four. That is a fact worth more than any guess.

choices.label: Walk down to the old pool entrance and think.
Sit on the viewing gallery steps and lay it all out.
Go home and look at the medal under a bright lamp.

nodes.body: Six events, six plaques, one initial on each. The paper has four crossed out in the same ink, the library plaque says 'THIRD EVENT' and gives one of them. That leaves an order problem and four unknowns.

choices.label: Go after the plaques themselves.
Go after the people who were on the team.

nodes.body: Miss Holloway is eighty-four. She lives in the old school house and cannot hold onto what day it is. She can still name every child in every swim team photo without pausing, and the event they swam best.

nodes.body: The viewing gallery steps stay dry under the overhang. They are wide enough to lay out the medal, the plaque, the photos, and the receipts side by side. Laid out like that, they stop being odd scraps and start being a list.

nodes.body: Under the bright kitchen lamp at home, the clasp gives up one more mark that the dim lost-property light never showed. A seventh, tiny scratch. It is not a place at all but a small, careful arrow pointing back at the first dot.

nodes.body: Six walls, one cage, and a rose bush stand between here and six brass rectangles. A plaque in your hand is an initial nobody can argue about. That is worth more today than any amount of being told things.

choices.label: Get the noticeboard off the office wall.
Find the plaque in the coach's garden.

nodes.body: Twenty-two children stood on those tiles in 1974, and twelve of them stood in the drizzle in 1998. The ones still in town are within a mile of this bench. Mostly indoors. Mostly glad to be asked.

He filed his own name off it because he thought he had let the team down. He had not. The corridor outside the cottage seems to know this fact before the residents do.

By ten to four on the last afternoon, there is a single sheet. It has six events, six initials, two orders, and every source for each. A copy of it goes through the library letterbox. Whatever happens at four o'clock, the trail itself is now something that cannot be thrown into a bin bag.

Behind the door is a relay trophy with a loose handle. There are four boxes. A stack of results sheets has gone to grey pulp along one edge. A typed card is taped to the inside of the door. It says the team will be back. It is less than the town remembers, and more than the clipboard was told.

The van is early. The men are quick. The store is empty by twenty past four, and the bin bags go out of the school drive at half past with a relay trophy in them that no one photographed. The padlock, still locked, is left hanging on the open hasp.

The store is emptied on schedule, with a list made first. So four boxes, a minute book, and a tin of photographs come out before the bin bags do, and everything else goes. It is not the afternoon anyone hoped for. It is not the afternoon that would have happened.

The six initials spell a name, the way a old coach would say it. The name of the first swimmer to win a County Final for the school. Once that is seen, it cannot be unseen. It is also seen at ten past four on the last afternoon, which is ten minutes after the van.

Nobody with authority is standing in the sunken garden at four o'clock. The folder is in a bag on a kitchen table across town. The store is cleared by twenty past. The padlock, which was the whole problem, was never actually the problem.

The name in the medal case is a grandma from the next street. She swam until she was eighteen. She has not said this out loud in fifty years. She takes the case back, and then after two weeks she brings it to the walk.

ending.title: A Medal Case With a Name In It

nodes.body: Two copies, one name on each, a list of eleven things, and a date. Done on the last afternoon in the school hall with the old folk watching. It is the least tense twenty minutes of the whole week. It is also the only reason nothing falls apart later.

A minute book from 1965, four hundred photos, a set of programmes, and one card that says 'COUNTY FINALS'. It is listed, numbered, and on a shelf with a date stamp on the back of each page. Mr Chen puts the medal photo in the case by the door.

Mr Harris leaves the plaque uncovered and moves the noticeboard a foot to the left. For about a month, people come into the caretaker's office to look at a piece of brass. Then they stop. The plaque stays.

The story runs on Friday under a photo of an empty shop and a pile of bin bags. It is a good piece of writing about a past event. Four people write in to say they would have helped, if someone had asked them on Tuesday.

Eleven walkers, one borrowed cup, a copied map, and six brass signs. The group stops at all six spots in the sun. They talk loudly at each one. More people follow it around than anyone thought. Half of them are under twelve.

Forty people walk the route on a Saturday in May. They follow an old woman of eighty-four. She stops at each sign and tells who stood there. At the bike shed, with no sign at all, everyone stands under the plastic roof and still listens.

Five plaques go back onto five walls with the right screws. The sixth is cut new in brass by a man on the industrial estate who will not take money for it. It goes onto the bike shed wall, in the square that has been waiting decades.

ending.title: Six Plaques Back on Six Walls

nodes.body: The medal goes back in its case. The scrap of paper is folded into a tiny square and put beside it. The case lives on a shelf. It is the only thing in the story that ends up right where it began, and means something totally different.

ending.title: The Medal Goes Back in Its Case

nodes.body: Trophies go to the museum. Paper to the library. A photo to the cottage. Plaques to the walls. The medal case goes to the archive with a note saying who found it. It takes three weeks of small, dull jobs. In the end, nothing is left in a bag under anyone's bed.

The store comes out onto the grass. It gets listed, shot with a camera, and split into 'keep' and 'bin bag'. Two men who are paid by the hour do this, and they are oddly keen. The room under the starting block ends the day swept, dry, and empty.

The van leaves the school drive at ten past four with a relay trophy and four boxes in it. There is a photograph of it going, taken from the gate. The Observer will not print it, because there is nothing to say about it.

ending.title: The Van on the Last Afternoon

nodes.body: Three separate adults would have stopped it. None of them were told, because asking felt like a bigger thing on Tuesday than it turned out to be on the following Monday, when all three said so in turn.

The last order is wrong. The dials go back to zero. The trail that ran from a lost-property crate through six walls and fifty years ends at a steel door in a sunken garden, with a van booked for four o'clock.

ending.title: The Trail Ends at a Steel Door
